title: TA8-20761
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXXXX and her minor daughter, XXXXX, citizens of the People's Republic of China (China), claim refugee protection pursuant to ss 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).
The principal claimant was appointed as the designated representative for her daughter, XXXXX who was seventeen years old at the time of the hearing.
The principal claimant (henceforth referred to as the claimant) alleges the following:

The claimant's husband came to Canada as a skilled worker and was granted permanent resident status. Tragically, he was killed by a car while riding his bicycle to work on XXXXX, 2006. When the claimant learned of the death, she was distraught. When the claimant invited her husband's family to discuss the funeral arrangements, all they were interested in was discussing her husband's financial situation and whether he had purchased life insurance. They also wanted her to borrow money from her company for plane tickets and the funeral, which the claimant could not do. Instead, the claimant borrowed money from her relatives, friends and co-workers. One of her husband's brothers, XXXXX, wanted her to pay for his trip for the funeral in Canada, as his family had no money. On XXXXX, 2006, the claimant was granted a visa to come to Canada while XXXXX visa was refused. The brother-in-law did not want them to go until he could obtain his visa, no matter how long it took. When the claimant accompanied her daughter to obtain her visa, XXXXX tried to stop them from entering the embassy. They eventually managed to obtain the visa. The claimant's father-in-law came one day with his other son, XXXXX, and insisted that he had expected his eldest son to take care of him, but that since he is dead, the claimant had to give him the $250,000 compensation money and money from donations and had to buy a house for him. XXXXX insisted that if the claimant did not give them the money, he would take her passport and not return it. He pushed the claimant to the edge of the bed and kept yelling at her.

On XXXXX, 2006, the claimant received a call from the president of the Canadian Shandong Association (CSA). The CSA had raised money for the claimants' trip and funeral costs. The president informed her that XXXXX had contacted her and asked that the CSA obtain a visa for his father and that the donated funds be sent to his father and his family. XXXXX said that he would not allow the claimants to leave China unless the CSA guaranteed that the funds would go to the claimant's husband's family. The president advised them to leave their home immediately, which they did the following morning.

When the claimant arrived in Canada, she learned that her husband's family were searching for the claimant and making threats that they would break their legs and even kill them unless they got the money. The claimant's father-in-law kept sending e-mails to the CSA asking for money. Also, he twice called the president asking about the claimants and trying to get their address. He said that he would get a visa and come to Canada to find the claimants.

The claimants received an insurance payment in the amount of $41,000. They also received $69,000 in donations. There is a claim before the courts which has not been settled. Her husband's family does not believe that the claimant has not received a huge settlement of $250,000 and keep asking for money.

The claimant fears that her husband's family may cripple or even kill them if they go back to China. The claimant feels that she cannot move to another area of China because she could not obtain a resident registration without property or a job. She also fears that her husband's family would easily find them. The claimant also fears that the police and authorities in China would not help them as they would regard the case as merely a family disagreement. They would only intervene if something serious were to happen.
I determine that the claimants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection. ANALYSIS Identity
The claimants' identities are established by their testimony and the documentation filed.1

In arriving at my decision, I have been aware of the difficulties faced by a claimant in providing testimony through an interpreter in the unfamiliar milieu of a Canadian hearing room. I have also considered the Chairperson's Gender Guidelines2 in considering the facts of this case. Section 96 of IRPA - Nexus

The determinative factor is whether there is nexus to any of the grounds under the definition of s. 96. Counsel has argued that the claimants are being persecuted because of their gender as they belong to a special social group of females fearing domestic violence.

I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimants are not being persecuted because of their gender. The minor claimant has testified that she was never treated well by her father's family because she is a girl and that they did not treat her very nicely or ignored her. There was no other evidence of mistreatment. I, therefore find, on a balance of probabilities, that what the minor claimant suffered was discrimination and not persecution.

I also find, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant did not suffer persecution in the past, but only discrimination. The claimant testified that she did not have good relations with her husband's family because they were disappointed that she and her husband did not have a son. She and her husband had decided not to jeopardize their jobs and positions in having a second child, which was contrary to the Chinese One Child policy and they also did not want to get rid of their daughter in order to have a son. The claimant also testified that her husband had been supporting his father and his two brothers' families, who had lost their jobs due to the one child policy. The claimant gave no evidence that she was persecuted in the past by her family because of her gender. The claimant testified that there was one incident after her husband's death when her brother-in-law pushed her and tried to take her passport. The claimant did not say she was injured. The claimant did not give her passport to her in-laws. I find that had her brother-in-law and father-in-law wanted to take her passport they could have overpowered her, but they did not. Even in regard to this incident, I do not find that the physical actions were because of the claimant's gender but because the claimant's in-laws wanted to achieve their goal of guaranteeing that they received money they felt was due them.

The question is whether the claimant would be persecuted by her husband's family because of her gender if she returns to China. The claimant testified that she tried to involve her husband's family in planning her husband's funeral. Instead of receiving sympathy, her in-laws were only concerned about going to the funeral themselves and getting life insurance money and donated money raised for the claimant. The claimant's brother-in-law tried to prevent her and her daughter from leaving China until he could get a visa. Later, the claimant's father in law tried to get the CSA that had raised money for the claimants to guarantee that they would remit half of the money to him. The claimant did not adduce any evidence whether her husband's family has any entitlement to this money under China's succession laws. She was specifically asked at the hearing if she knew if her in-laws had any legal entitlement to the money from her husband's estate. The claimant replied that she does not know and did not inquire about any entitlement they may have. If they do not, then what the family is attempting to do is to extort money from the claimant by threatening her and her daughter. I find, on a balance of probabilities, that if her husband's family is threatening them, it is not because they are female members of a particular social group, but because they want to obtain the money, some of which they may or may not be entitled to.

I also find, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimants do not have membership in a social group of women suffering domestic violence. The claimants never adduced any evidence that they suffered any persecution within the family because of their relationship to family members, only discrimination. I have already found that what the claimants fear is persecution because of possible extortion and not domestic violence because of their relationship within the family. Section 97 - Risk to life

The claimant alleges that her husband's family has threatened to break their legs and even kill them if they do not hand over the large amount of life insurance and other moneys to which they feel they are entitled. However, the question remains whether these threats were genuine or whether they were empty threats uttered in the heat of the moment and whether they would be acted upon.

The claimants arrived in Canada in XXXXX 2006 and made their refugee claims in October 2008, some two and a half years after arrival. The claimants made every attempt to stay in Canada. Their application for a visitor's visa extension was refused. The claimant testified that it was her late husband's intention to bring her and her daughter to Canada and that he was saving money for that purpose. The minor claimant also indicated that she wanted to fulfill her father's dream by remaining in Canada and obtaining an education in Canada. The claimants made an application for Permanent Residency based on Humanitarian and Compassionate (H&C) grounds, but that application was refused. The reasons stated for pursuing the H&C application is that the claimants wished to stay in Canada because that was their dream and because their application for compensation is still before the courts and because the claimants would have problems re-establishing themselves after returning to China. The claimants applied for judicial review of that decision, but were unsuccessful. At no time during the H&C application did the claimants indicate that they were fearful of returning home to China because of the threats of their husband/father's family.

The claimant testified that the Immigration officer who interviewed them suggested they make a refugee claim. The claimant further testified that up to that point she was unaware that she could make a refugee claim. I do not accept this explanation as the claimants had legal advice in reference to their H&C application and appeal and would have, on the balance of probabilities, been advised of their options. I find, therefore, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimants lacked subjective fear. State Protection

I find that the determinative issue in this case is whether the claimants have rebutted the presumption of state protection. Even if the claimant's husband's family has the intention to harm the claimants, I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimants have not provided clear and convincing proof that state protection would not be available to them.

There is a presumption that a state is capable of protecting its citizens except in situations where the state is in a state of complete breakdown.3 To rebut the presumption of state protection, a claimant must provide clear and convincing evidence of the state's inability to protect absent an admission by the national's state of its inability to protect that national.4 While the effectiveness of the protection is a relevant consideration, the test is whether the protection offered is adequate.5 The evidence that state protection is not adequate must be reliable and probative and it must also satisfy me, on a balance of probabilities, that the state protection is inadequate.6 The claimant must approach the state for protection, providing that state protection might be reasonably forthcoming.7 Where a state is in effective control of its territory, has military, police and civil authority in place and makes serious efforts to protect its citizens, the mere fact it is not always successful at doing so will not be enough to justify a claim that the victims are unable to avail themselves of protection.8 The fact that state protection is not perfect9 does not constitute clear and convincing proof of the state's inability to protect its citizens, since no state can guarantee the protection of all its citizens at all times. Local failures to provide effective policing do not amount to a lack of state protection unless they are part of a broader pattern of the state's inability to provide protection.10 The burden of proof that rests on the claimant increases with the level of democracy of the state in question. The more democratic a state is, the more the claimant must have done to exhaust all course of action open to them to demonstrate state protection was or would not be forthcoming.11

Clearly, China is not a democracy. On the other hand, through its laws and practice, there is little doubt that the government of China rules the country. If the government determines to provide state protection, it has the law enforcement structure and ability to do so, to whatever extent it might prioritize the issue. China has a functioning judiciary and police force. State protection has been determined to be an element of Chinese society and legal system in the oft-cited case of Xue.12 The claimant must do what she can to access the available protection, particularly as the alleged persecution in this case is not at the hands of the state and the state is making efforts to combat serious domestic abuse as well as criminality.

I have found above that the claimants' claim is not appropriately based on a Convention ground. In case I am incorrect in my analysis, I have considered state protection in relation to domestic violence. Based upon the country documents, there is a level of state protection for the victims of serious domestic violence in China. Country documentation13 indicates that violence against women continues to be a serious problem in China. China is taking steps to improve the situation for abused spouses. However, the claimants' fear of domestic violence is not of a continuing persecution but is specifically related to the one issue in regard to the money the claimants may or may not obtain. Most of the programs set up to aid women suffering domestic abuse in China, are therefore likely not applicable to the claimants, although they would still be able to use the services. For example, there are a growing number of shelters in China available for victims of domestic abuse, legal aid service centers and special police booths for domestic violence complaints. Although there is no national law criminalizing domestic violence, the criminal law, marriage law, and other laws on public security provide for mediation and administrative penalties in cases of domestic violence. The claimants could avail themselves of these avenues of protection, if necessary, while seeking redress through the legal system. I find that the claimant has not adduced relevant, reliable and convincing evidence which satisfies me, the trier of fact, on a balance of probabilities, that the state protection available in China to the claimants from the threats of their husband's/father's family, is inadequate.

I find that the claimant made no attempts to seek state protection while in China. I accept that the claimant was extremely distressed because of the death of her husband and was focused on reaching Canada to deal with her husband's death and funeral. The claimant, however, has been in Canada for four years and therefore had the opportunity to report the threats from her husband's family to the Chinese government through her own family who remain in China or through the Chinese embassy or consulate and to seek their advice. The claimant even submitted a photograph of herself with the Chinese consul in Canada. In addition, the claimant has testified that she has not informed herself of the Chinese succession laws to see if her husband's family has any legitimate claims to any money due to her husband's estate. I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant has not shown that state protection is not available to her and her daughter.

The claimant is an intelligent, well-educated woman who had a responsible job in China. I would expect that the claimant could re-establish herself in China. Apparently, her own family lives a three hour drive from her in-laws and that is where the claimants resided before coming to Canada. The claimant testified that she could not move anywhere in China where her in-laws could not find her. The claimant testified that her sister-in-law had two brothers who were members of the Public Security Bureau (PSB) and that they would help her husband's family to locate the claimants even if they moved to a different part of the country. When the claimant was asked how she knew that they would help to locate her and daughter, she replied that they would do so because her husband's family is desperate for money. I find that this is mere speculation on the part of the claimant. I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimants could relocate in a different part of the country to be away from their alleged persecutors. The claimant also presented no evidence that these two PSB officials, one of whom works in an unnamed prison, could prevent the claimant from obtaining protection. I do not conclude, based on the claimant's evidence and on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant's husband's family has the means to effectively block state protection.

The elements necessary to establish a claim under s. 97 (1) of the IRPA are not identical to those necessary to establish whether a person is a Convention refugee under s. 96 of the IRPA. A determination of a refugee claim under s. 96 of the IRPA, is not necessarily determinative of a claim under subsection 97 (1) of the IRPA.14 However, in the case at hand, whether the claim is framed under s. 96 or s. 97 of the IRPA, I find that there is state protection available to the claimants.

I have concluded that state protection is available to the claimants. As a result, I am of the opinion that there is not more than a mere possibility that, should the claimants return to China, they would face persecution or, on the balance of probabilities, be in danger of torture or at risk to their lives or at risk of being subjected to cruel and unusual treatment or punishment.

For the foregoing reasons, I conclude that the claimants are not Convention refugees and not persons in need of protection. The Refugee Protection Division therefore rejects their claims.
